title: Designing Request Bodies
learning_outcomes: Explain how designing request bodies affects an API contract or implementation.
Apply the key ideas from create request schemas to a concrete API example.
Identify one failure, security, or compatibility risk and describe how to verify it.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on designing request bodies in json and data representations. You will connect create request schemas to a concrete API contract decision, inspect a small example, and decide what evidence proves the behavior is correct.
content.why_it_matters: Designing Request Bodies matters because API consumers depend on predictable behavior even when clients, servers, networks, and stored data evolve independently. Applying create request schemas deliberately reduces ambiguity, makes failures easier to diagnose, and gives tests a clear expectation.

content_blocks.title: Lesson 57 concept map
content_blocks.alt_text: Lesson 57: Create request schemas → Update request schemas → Read-only and server-generated fields → Optional, required, and nullable fields.
content_blocks.caption: Follow the 4 syllabus topics in order, then inspect the example.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: JSON is a representation format; decide types, nullability, field exposure, and compatibility as part of the public schema. In this lesson, treat “Designing Request Bodies” as a design or implementation decision: name the expected behavior, identify its boundary, and verify it with a representative request or test.

content_blocks.title: Inspect the pattern: Designing Request Bodies
content_blocks.expected_output: The JSON object has stable public fields, typed values, an explicit nullable date, and a collection of tags.

content_blocks.title: Walkthrough
content_blocks.text: Start with “Create request schemas”; it establishes the vocabulary for this topic. Next, compare it with “Update request schemas” and “Optional, required, and nullable fields”. In a real API, write down the observable behavior first, then test one normal request and one invalid or unauthorized request. Keep resource state, caller identity, and internal implementation details separate.

content_blocks.title: Professional review check
content_blocks.text: Treat a response body as a public contract; never leak internal persistence fields by default. The worked snippet is intentionally inspectable, not an executable hosted API. Replace example.test and placeholder identifiers with local test data only when you implement the lesson project.

content.task: Create a small design note or request/response example demonstrating designing request bodies. Use the subtopics above to explain the intended behavior, the main edge case, and the evidence you would use to verify it.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the role of “Create request schemas” in this API topic.
Provide a concrete resource, request, response, schema, test, or operational example as appropriate.
Identify one failure/security/compatibility edge case and a test or check for it.
content.expected_output: A reviewable example for Designing Request Bodies with a clear expected behavior and at least one verifiable edge case.
content.run_instructions: Execution mode: static-validation. This lesson example is a protocol, schema, SQL, or code fragment for inspection; it is not submitted to a production server and CodeLeaf does not execute arbitrary learner code. Validate JSON/YAML with a local linter or run the relevant HTTP request against the isolated service you implement for a project. Do not send illustrative example.test requests to a real service.
content.reset_steps: Use a disposable local database or test fixture for implementation work. Restore seed data between runs; never point exercises at production customer data or live payment endpoints.
troubleshooting: Check the exact HTTP method, path, status, header, media type, and payload before changing implementation code.
Separate a transport failure from an application validation failure, authorization denial, and dependency/database failure.
Confirm the example and its client tooling version are compatible; consult the linked standard or official guidance when behavior is ambiguous.
common_mistakes: Treating designing request bodies as an implementation detail rather than a documented behavior.
Testing only the happy path and ignoring malformed, unauthorized, conflicting, duplicate, or dependency-failure cases.
Publishing an example without checking version assumptions, sensitive-data exposure, and the expected output.
summary: JSON is a representation format; decide types, nullability, field exposure, and compatibility as part of the public schema. In this lesson, treat “Designing Request Bodies” as a design or implementation decision: name the expected behavior, identify its boundary, and verify it with a representative request or test.
Next, connect this idea to Lesson 58: JSON Data Type Decisions.
